drills.title: Build the music chart
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines (and indent them) so the program prints the songs from most played to least played, with a rank. Two lines do not belong.
lines: chart = sorted(songs, key=lambda s: s[1], reverse=True)
for rank, (title, plays) in enumerate(chart, start=1):
drills.explain: sorted() builds a new, ordered list. key= must be a function that returns what to sort by, so it needs lambda s: s[1] (key=s[1] fails because s does not exist outside the lambda). Without reverse=True the least played song would come first. enumerate(chart, start=1) hands you the rank and the item together, and the (title, plays) in the loop header unpacks each tuple.
drills.output:
1. Heeriye (1200 plays)
2. Kesariya (900 plays)
3. Tum Hi Ho (400 plays)

drills.title: Filter and transform in one line
drills.prompt: Fill the three blanks to finish the comprehensions: one filters the catalog by budget, one chooses a label for every price.
code: names = [name ___ name, price in prices.items() ___ price <= budget]
labels = ["cheap" ___ p < 500 else "pricey" for p in prices.values()]
drills.explain: The pattern is [what_to_keep for item in source if condition]. The if at the end filters: items that fail it are left out. An if/else that changes the value goes in front of the for, because every item still produces a result ("cheap" or "pricey").

drills.title: Ties and sort keys
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
code: print([title for title, plays in chart])
drills.explain: A tuple key sorts by its first item and breaks ties with the second. The minus sign puts the biggest plays first, and the title then sorts the 900-play songs A to Z. max() with a tie returns the first of the equal items it meets, so Kesariya wins. sorted() is stable: with reverse=True, items of equal length (bb and dd) keep their original order.

drills.title: The if/else in the wrong place
drills.prompt: The program stops with an error before it prints anything. Click the faulty line and choose the fix.
code: result = ["pass" for m in marks if m >= 40 else "fail"]
options: result = ["pass" if m >= 40 else "fail" for m in marks]
result = ["pass" for m in marks if m >= 40]
result = ["pass" if m >= 40 for m in marks else "fail"]
result = ["pass" for m in marks if m >= 40 elif "fail"]
fixed_code: result = ["pass" if m >= 40 else "fail" for m in marks]
drills.explain: A trailing if only filters, and it cannot have an else. When each item must become one of two values, put the if/else in front of the for: [value_a if condition else value_b for item in source]. The second option runs but drops the failing marks instead of labelling them.

drills.title: Review the AI's product filter
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this filter for an e-commerce page. It runs, but tick the statements that point at real problems.
code: affordable = [p["name"] for p in catalog if p["price"] <= budget]

issues.text: sorted(...)[0] with the default order returns the LOWEST rated product, not the best
issues.why: sorted() goes from small to large. Take the last item, add reverse=True, or simply use max(catalog, key=lambda p: p["rating"]), which also avoids sorting everything to pick one item.

issues.text: A list comprehension is used only to print, and builds a throw-away list of None
issues.why: Comprehensions are for building lists. Use a normal for loop when the goal is a side effect such as printing.

non_issues.text: A lambda is not allowed as the key= argument
non_issues.why: key= expects a function, and a short lambda is the usual way to pick the field to sort by.

non_issues.text: sorted() reorders catalog, so the later loop sees a different order
non_issues.why: sorted() returns a new list and leaves the original untouched. (list.sort() is the one that changes the list in place.)

non_issues.text: The comprehension must be written as a for loop with append
non_issues.why: A filter with one condition fits comfortably on one line, which is exactly the use case for a comprehension.

drills.explain: Review comprehension code for two things: does the sort order or the filter match the requirement (ascending vs descending, < vs <=), and is a comprehension being used for what it is meant for, building a list? sorted(...)[0] is a frequent AI slip because it looks right and runs without errors.
